notes.front: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)?
notes.back: An extra layer of security at sign-in: besides your username and password, you give a second form of authentication only you know or have.
notes.explanation: It adds a second check, something only you know or have, on top of your username and password.
notes.example: Like a bank card that also needs a secret code: someone who steals only the card still cannot use it.
notes.evidence: Two-factor authentication (2FA) is an extra layer of security used when logging into websites or apps. With 2FA, you have to log in with your username and password and provide another form of authentication that only you know or have access to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: What are 2FA recovery codes?
notes.back: Codes you download and save when you set up 2FA, which let you sign in to GitHub if you lose access to your phone.
notes.explanation: They are a way back into the account when the usual second factor is gone.
notes.example: Like a spare house key left with a trusted neighbour in case you lose your own.
notes.evidence: When you configure two-factor authentication, you'll download and save your 2FA recovery codes. If you lose access to your phone, you can authenticate to GitHub using your recovery codes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”, “Two-factor authentication recovery codes”

notes.front: What is a passkey on GitHub?
notes.back: A way to sign in to GitHub in your browser without typing your password.
notes.explanation: If you use 2FA, a passkey satisfies both the password and the 2FA requirement, so sign-in takes a single step.
notes.example: Like unlocking your phone with your fingerprint instead of typing a code.
notes.evidence: Passkeys allow you to sign in securely to GitHub in your browser, without having to input your password. If you use two-factor authentication (2FA), passkeys satisfy both password and 2FA requirements, so you can complete your sign in with a single step.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About passkeys”, “About passkeys”

notes.front: What is the Triage role for an organization repository?
notes.back: The role recommended for contributors who need to proactively manage issues, discussions and pull requests without write access.
notes.explanation: It sits between Read and Write in the list of repository roles.
notes.example: Like a library volunteer who sorts and tags returned books but may not rewrite them.
notes.evidence: Triage: Recommended for contributors who need to proactively manage issues, discussions, and pull requests without write access
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: What is the Maintain role for an organization repository?
notes.back: The role recommended for project managers who need to manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions.
notes.explanation: It sits between Write and Admin; Admin is the role that adds the sensitive and destructive actions.
notes.example: Like a building manager who runs the day-to-day but cannot sell or demolish the building.
notes.evidence: Maintain: Recommended for project managers who need to manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions * Admin: Recommended for people who need full access to the project, including sensitive and destructive actions
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: What is an outside collaborator in an organization?
notes.back: A person with access to one or more organization repositories who is not explicitly a member of the organization.
notes.explanation: The docs give a consultant or a temporary employee as examples.
notes.example: Like a visiting contractor given a key to one office, without becoming staff.
notes.evidence: An outside collaborator is a person who has access to one or more organization repositories but is not explicitly a member of the organization, such as a consultant or temporary employee.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Outside collaborators”

notes.front: What is a custom organization role?
notes.back: A role you create to let a member administer certain subsets of organization settings, without full administrative control.
notes.explanation: The docs' example is a role containing the "View organization audit log" permission; the feature is only for organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.example: Like giving an office worker a key to the records room but not to the whole building.
notes.evidence: Organization roles are a way to grant an organization member the ability to administer certain subsets of settings without granting full administrative control of the organization and its repositories. For example, you could create a role that contains the "View organization audit log" permission. This feature is only available to organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “About custom organization roles”

notes.front: What is an identity provider (IdP), in GitHub's enterprise docs?
notes.back: An external identity management system from which an enterprise manages its users' lifecycle and authentication.
notes.explanation: With Enterprise Managed Users, the enterprise manages its GitHub users from its IdP.
notes.example: Like a company's staff directory that issues and cancels every employee's building pass.
notes.evidence: With Enterprise Managed Users, you manage the lifecycle and authentication of your users on GitHub.com or GHE.com from an external identity management system, or IdP
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”

notes.front: What is Enterprise Managed Users (EMU)?
notes.back: An enterprise set-up in which you manage your GitHub users' lifecycle and authentication from your IdP.
notes.explanation: The IdP provisions the user accounts, and users must authenticate on the IdP to reach the enterprise's resources.
notes.example: Like a company laptop pool: the company creates, controls and retires every account, not the staff.
notes.evidence: With Enterprise Managed Users, you manage the lifecycle and authentication of your users on GitHub.com or GHE.com from an external identity management system, or IdP : * Your IdP provisions new user accounts on GitHub, with access to your enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”

notes.front: What is a Copilot policy in an organization?
notes.back: A setting that controls which GitHub Copilot features and models are available to users who get a licence through the organization.
notes.explanation: Copilot policies are also managed at the enterprise level.
notes.example: Like a school deciding which apps pupils may use on the tablets it hands out.
notes.evidence: Control the availability of GitHub Copilot features and models for users granted a license by your organization. Copilot policies are also managed at the enterprise level.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization”

notes.front: What is a branch protection rule?
notes.back: A rule that protects an important branch by deciding whether collaborators can delete or force push to it, and setting requirements for pushes.
notes.explanation: Requirements can include passing status checks or a linear commit history.
notes.example: Like a signed-off master copy of a contract that nobody may overwrite without the agreed approvals.
notes.evidence: You can protect important branches by setting branch protection rules, which define whether collaborators can delete or force push to the branch and set requirements for any pushes to the branch, such as passing status checks or a linear commit history.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”

notes.front: What is a team in a GitHub organization?
notes.back: A group of organization members that reflects your company's or group's structure, with cascading access permissions and mentions.
notes.explanation: Access permissions and mentions cascade through a team.
notes.example: Like a department mailing list that also carries the department's door-key permissions.
notes.evidence: Teams are groups of organization members that reflect your company or group's structure with cascading access permissions and mentions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “About teams”

notes.front: What are nested teams?
notes.back: Teams arranged in several levels, parent and child, to reflect your group's or company's hierarchy.
notes.explanation: A parent team can have several child teams, but each child team has only one parent.
notes.example: Like a company chart where Engineering sits under Staff, and Mobile sits under Engineering.
notes.evidence: You can reflect your group or company's hierarchy within your GitHub organization with multiple levels of nested teams. A parent team can have multiple child teams, while each child team only has one parent team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “Nested teams”

notes.front: For GitHub, what is the second form of authentication in 2FA?
notes.back: A code generated by an app on your mobile device, or sent as a text message.
notes.explanation: Once 2FA is on, GitHub generates an authentication code whenever someone tries to sign in to your account.
notes.evidence: For GitHub, the second form of authentication is a code that's generated by an application on your mobile device or sent as a text message (SMS). After you enable 2FA, GitHub generates an authentication code any time someone attempts to sign into your account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: Someone has stolen Ana's GitHub password, but not her phone. She has 2FA on with a one-time password app. Can they sign in?
choices: No: they also need the authentication code on her phone
Yes, once GitHub emails them a code
Only from a device Ana has used before
notes.back: No: they also need the authentication code on her phone.
notes.explanation: With 2FA, signing in needs both the password and access to the authentication code on the phone.

choicesExplained.Yes: the password is enough: With 2FA on, a password alone is not enough.
choicesExplained.Yes, once GitHub emails them a code: The second factor is a code on her phone, from an app or by text message, not an email.
choicesExplained.Only from a device Ana has used before: The docs make no exception for known devices; the code on her phone is still needed.

notes.evidence: The only way someone can sign into your account is if they know both your password and have access to the authentication code on your phone.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: Which 2FA method generates time-based one-time passwords in an app on your phone?
notes.back: A time-based one-time password mobile app.
notes.explanation: You configure 2FA with a one-time password app or by text message before you can add a security key.
notes.evidence: After you configure 2FA, using a time-based one-time password (TOTP) mobile app, or via text message, you can add a security key
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: Which 2FA method delivers your authentication code to your phone as a text message?
notes.back: Text messages.
notes.explanation: GitHub's second factor can be a code from an app or one sent as a text message.
notes.evidence: For GitHub, the second form of authentication is a code that's generated by an application on your mobile device or sent as a text message (SMS).
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: Which 2FA method, made possible by WebAuthn, can use Apple's fingerprint reader or Windows Hello?
notes.back: A security key.
notes.explanation: You can add a security key after configuring 2FA with a one-time password app or text messages.
notes.evidence: After you configure 2FA, using a time-based one-time password (TOTP) mobile app, or via text message, you can add a security key, like a FIDO2 hardware security key, Apple Touch ID or Windows Hello. The technology that enables authentication with a security key is called WebAuthn.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: Which 2FA method lets any mobile device you have signed in to its app act as your second factor, using public-key cryptography?
notes.back: GitHub Mobile.
notes.explanation: You can use GitHub Mobile for 2FA once a one-time password app or text messages are configured.
notes.evidence: You can also use GitHub Mobile for 2FA after configuring a TOTP mobile app or text messages. GitHub Mobile uses public-key cryptography to secure your account, allowing you to use any mobile device that you've used to sign in to GitHub Mobile as your second factor.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: What is the technology that enables authentication with a security key called?
notes.back: WebAuthn.
notes.explanation: The docs say WebAuthn works in all modern browsers.
notes.evidence: The technology that enables authentication with a security key is called WebAuthn. WebAuthn is the successor to U2F and works in all modern browsers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: You have 2FA on, and lose both your 2FA credentials and your recovery methods. Can GitHub Support restore your access?
notes.back: No: GitHub Support will not be able to restore access, for security reasons.
notes.explanation: The warning covers accounts with 2FA enabled whose owners lose their credentials or recovery methods.
notes.evidence: For security reasons, GitHub Support will not be able to restore access to accounts with two-factor authentication enabled if you lose your two-factor authentication credentials or lose access to your account recovery methods.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”, “Two-factor authentication recovery codes”

notes.front: Ravi's phone, which holds his one-time password app, is stolen. He saved his codes when he set up 2FA. How can he sign in to GitHub?
choices: Ask GitHub Support to turn off 2FA
Sign in with his password alone
Create a new account with the same username
notes.back: Use his 2FA recovery codes.
notes.explanation: If you lose access to your phone, you can authenticate to GitHub using your recovery codes.

choicesExplained.Ask GitHub Support to turn off 2FA: GitHub Support will not be able to restore access to accounts with 2FA if the credentials and recovery methods are lost.
choicesExplained.Sign in with his password alone: With 2FA on, the password alone does not let anyone sign in.
choicesExplained.Create a new account with the same usern: That would not recover his existing account.

notes.evidence: If you lose access to your phone, you can authenticate to GitHub using your recovery codes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”, “Two-factor authentication recovery codes”

notes.front: Whom can organization owners require to use 2FA?
notes.back: Organization members, billing managers and outside collaborators.
notes.explanation: The requirement secures these people's personal accounts.
notes.evidence: Organization owners can require that organization members, billing managers, and outside collaborators use two-factor authentication to secure their personal accounts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”, “Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization”

notes.front: Passkeys are similar to security keys and satisfy both {{c1::password and 2FA}} requirements, allowing you to sign in with a single step.
notes.back: password and 2FA
notes.explanation: The docs describe passkeys as similar to security keys.
notes.evidence: Passkeys are similar to security keys and satisfy both password and 2FA requirements, allowing you to sign in with a single step.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: If you add a passkey, what else do the docs say you should configure, and why?
notes.back: A fallback 2FA method, such as a one-time password app or text messages, to reduce the risk of account lockouts.
notes.explanation: The docs pair the passkey option with this advice straight away.
notes.evidence: However, to reduce the risk of account lockouts, you should also configure a fallback 2FA method, such as a TOTP mobile app or SMS-based authentication.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About two-factor authentication”

notes.front: If you don't use 2FA, what does signing in with a passkey let you skip?
notes.back: The requirement to verify a new device by email.
notes.explanation: You can also use passkeys for sudo mode and for resetting your password.
notes.evidence: If you don't use 2FA, using a passkey will skip the requirement to verify a new device via email. You can also use passkeys for sudo mode and resetting your password.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About passkeys”, “About passkeys”

notes.front: What is a passkey made of, and where is it kept?
notes.back: A pair of cryptographic keys, one public and one private, stored by an authenticator you control.
notes.explanation: The authenticator proves you are present and authorised, with a passcode, personal code, biometric or device password.
notes.evidence: Passkeys are pairs of cryptographic keys (a public key and a private key) that are stored by an authenticator you control. The authenticator can prove that a user is present and is authorized to use the passkey. Authenticators prove authorization with a PIN, passcode, biometric, or device password
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About passkeys”, “About passkeys”

notes.front: Why are passkeys highly phishing-resistant?
notes.back: They are bound to a website domain and need a secure connection, so the browser refuses to authenticate to a lookalike site.
notes.explanation: The docs contrast this with text-message or one-time-password 2FA, which can be phished.
notes.evidence: Passkeys are bound to a website domain, like GitHub.com , and require a secure connection, meaning that the web browser will refuse to authenticate to a lookalike phishing website. These properties make passkeys highly phishing-resistant, and much harder to attack than SMS or TOTP 2FA, which can be phished.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About passkeys”, “About passkeys”

notes.front: Lena already uses 2FA and wants to sign in to GitHub in one step, without typing her password, with something much harder to phish than a text-message code. What should she add?
notes.back: A passkey.
notes.explanation: A passkey satisfies both password and 2FA requirements, so sign-in takes a single step.

choicesExplained.A second one-time password app: A one-time password code is still a second step after the password, and such codes can be phished.
choicesExplained.More recovery codes: Recovery codes are for getting back in after losing your phone, not for everyday sign-in.
choicesExplained.A saved reply: A saved reply is reusable text for issues and pull requests; it has nothing to do with signing in.

notes.evidence: If you use two-factor authentication (2FA), passkeys satisfy both password and 2FA requirements, so you can complete your sign in with a single step.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About passkeys”, “About passkeys”

notes.front: From least to most access, the roles for an organization repository are Read, {{c1::Triage}}, Write, Maintain and Admin.
notes.back: Triage
notes.explanation: Triage sits between Read and Write: it manages issues and pull requests without write access.
notes.evidence: From least access to most access, the roles for an organization repository are: * Read: Recommended for non-code contributors who want to view or discuss your project * Triage: Recommended for contributors who need to proactively manage issues, discussions, and pull requests without write access
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: Which organization repository role is recommended for non-code contributors who want to view or discuss the project?
notes.back: Read.
notes.explanation: Read is the role with the least access.
notes.evidence: From least access to most access, the roles for an organization repository are: * Read: Recommended for non-code contributors who want to view or discuss your project
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: Which organization repository role is recommended for contributors who actively push to the project?
notes.back: Write.
notes.explanation: Write comes after Triage and before Maintain in the list of roles.
notes.evidence: Write: Recommended for contributors who actively push to your project
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: Which organization repository role is needed for sensitive and destructive actions such as managing security or deleting the repository?
notes.back: Admin.
notes.explanation: Admin is recommended for people who need full access to the project.
notes.evidence: Admin: Recommended for people who need full access to the project, including sensitive and destructive actions like managing security or deleting a repository
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: A community helper will label, sort and close issues and pull requests in an organization repository but should not push code. Which role fits with the least access?
notes.back: Triage.
notes.explanation: Triage is for contributors who proactively manage issues, discussions and pull requests without write access.

choicesExplained.Write: Write is for contributors who actively push, which this helper should not do.
choicesExplained.Maintain: Maintain is for project managers who manage the repository, more access than needed.
choicesExplained.Admin: Admin gives full access, including destructive actions.

notes.evidence: Triage: Recommended for contributors who need to proactively manage issues, discussions, and pull requests without write access
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: A project manager must manage an organization repository day to day but must not be able to delete it. Which role fits best?
notes.back: Maintain.
notes.explanation: Maintain lets a project manager manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions.

choicesExplained.Admin: Admin includes destructive actions such as deleting a repository.
choicesExplained.Triage: Triage manages issues, discussions and pull requests, not the repository itself.
choicesExplained.Read: Read is for viewing or discussing the project.

notes.evidence: Maintain: Recommended for project managers who need to manage the repository without access to sensitive or destructive actions
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: What do the docs advise when choosing a repository role for a person or team?
notes.back: Choose the role that best fits their function, without giving more access than they need.
notes.explanation: Roles can go to organization members, outside collaborators and teams.
notes.evidence: You can give organization members, outside collaborators, and teams of people different levels of access to repositories owned by an organization by assigning them to roles. Choose the role that best fits each person or team's function in your project without giving people more access to the project than they need.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: What access do organization owners have to the organization's repositories?
notes.back: Admin access to every repository the organization owns.
notes.explanation: Owners manage the organization-level settings as well.
notes.evidence: In addition to managing organization-level settings, organization owners have admin access to every repository owned by the organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Repository roles for an organization”, “Repository roles for organizations”

notes.front: How many permission levels does a repository owned by a personal account have, and what are they?
notes.back: Two: the repository owner and collaborators.
notes.explanation: For more granular access, the docs suggest transferring the repository to an organization.
notes.evidence: A repository owned by a personal account has two permission levels: the repository owner and collaborators. > \[!TIP] > If you require more granular access to a repository owned by your personal account, consider transferring the repository to an organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Permission levels for a personal account repository”

notes.front: Omar owns a private repository on his personal account and wants a friend to read the code but not change it. What can he do?
choices: Nothing in that repository: collaborators there can only get write access
Add the friend as a collaborator with Read
Add the friend as a collaborator with Triage
Make the friend an outside collaborator
notes.back: Nothing in that repository: collaborators on a personal account's private repository can only get write access.
notes.explanation: Collaborators can't have read-only access to repositories owned by a personal account.

choicesExplained.Add the friend as a collaborator with Re: Read-only access is not available to collaborators on a personal account's repository.
choicesExplained.Add the friend as a collaborator with Tr: Triage is a role for organization repositories, not personal ones.
choicesExplained.Make the friend an outside collaborator: Outside collaborators belong to organization repositories.

notes.evidence: In a private repository, repository owners can only grant write access to collaborators. Collaborators can't have read-only access to repositories owned by a personal account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Permission levels for a personal account repository”, “Collaborator access for a repository owned by a personal account”

notes.front: Can a collaborator on a personal account's repository rename the default branch?
notes.back: No: collaborators can rename a branch other than the default branch.
notes.explanation: Renaming branches is on the collaborators' list of actions, but only for branches other than the default.
notes.evidence: Rename a branch other than the default branch
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Permission levels for a personal account repository”, “Collaborator access for a repository owned by a personal account”

notes.front: On GitHub, what is the difference between a permission and a role?
notes.back: A permission is the ability to perform a specific action; a role is a set of permissions you assign to individuals or teams.
notes.explanation: The docs' example of a permission is the ability to delete an issue.
notes.evidence: A permission is the ability to perform a specific action. For example, the ability to delete an issue is a permission. A role is a set of permissions you can assign to individuals or teams.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “About roles”

notes.front: How many people should hold the organization owner role?
notes.back: It should be limited, but to no fewer than two people.
notes.explanation: Organization owners have complete administrative access to the organization.
notes.evidence: Organization owners have complete administrative access to your organization. This role should be limited, but to no less than two people, in your organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Organization owners”

notes.front: Which organization role is the default, non-administrative role, able by default to create repositories and projects?
notes.back: Organization member.
notes.explanation: Members start with a number of permissions by default, including creating repositories and projects.
notes.evidence: The default, non-administrative role for people in an organization is the organization member. By default, organization members have a number of permissions, including the ability to create repositories and projects.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Organization members”

notes.front: Which organization role lets members block non-member contributors, set interaction limits and hide comments in the organization's public repositories?
notes.back: Organization moderator.
notes.explanation: Moderators keep their member permissions and gain these moderation abilities.
notes.evidence: Moderators are organization members who, in addition to their permissions as members, are allowed to block and unblock non-member contributors, set interaction limits, and hide comments in public repositories owned by the organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Organization moderators”

notes.front: Which organization role manages billing settings, such as payment information?
notes.back: Billing manager.
notes.explanation: The docs call it useful where members don't usually have access to billing resources.
notes.evidence: Billing managers are users who can manage the billing settings for your organization, such as payment information. This is a useful option if members of your organization don't usually have access to billing resources.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Billing managers”

notes.front: A security team must view security alerts and manage security feature settings across an organization, with the least access needed. Which role should the owners assign?
notes.back: Security manager.
notes.explanation: The security manager role gives permission to view security alerts and manage security settings across the organization, plus read permission for all its repositories.

choicesExplained.Organization owner: Owners have complete administrative access, far more than needed.
choicesExplained.Billing manager: Billing managers manage billing settings, not security features.
choicesExplained.Organization moderator: Moderators block contributors, set interaction limits and hide comments.

notes.evidence: When applied, it gives permission to view security alerts and manage settings for security features across your organization, as well as read permission for all repositories in the organization. If your organization has a security team, you can use the security manager role to give members of the team the least access they need to the organization.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Security managers”

notes.front: A company hires a consultant for three months to work in two of its organization's repositories. How should it give her access without making her a member?
choices: Add her as an outside collaborator
notes.back: Add her as an outside collaborator.
notes.explanation: An outside collaborator has access to one or more organization repositories without being a member, such as a consultant.

choicesExplained.Add her to a team: Teams are made up only of organization members; outside collaborators cannot be on a team.
choicesExplained.Make her a billing manager: Billing managers manage billing settings, not repository work.
choicesExplained.Make her an organization owner: Owners have complete administrative access to the organization.

notes.evidence: An outside collaborator is a person who has access to one or more organization repositories but is not explicitly a member of the organization, such as a consultant or temporary employee.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Roles in an organization”, “Outside collaborators”

notes.front: With Enterprise Managed Users, where must users authenticate to reach the enterprise's resources on GitHub?
notes.back: On the enterprise's IdP.
notes.explanation: The IdP also provisions the user accounts on GitHub.
notes.evidence: Users must authenticate on your IdP to access your enterprise's resources on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”

notes.front: With Enterprise Managed Users, what are two things you control from your IdP?
notes.back: Any two of: usernames, profile data, organization membership, repository access.
notes.explanation: Under Enterprise Managed Users, these are managed from the IdP.
notes.evidence: You control usernames, profile data, organization membership, and repository access from your IdP.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”

notes.front: A developer with a managed user account in an EMU enterprise wants to publish a public repository and help on a project outside the enterprise. What happens?
choices: She can't: managed user accounts cannot create public content or collaborate outside the enterprise
She can, once her IdP approves it
She can, but only with 2FA on
She can create public content but not collaborate outside
notes.back: She can't: managed user accounts cannot create public content or collaborate outside the enterprise.
notes.explanation: This is one of the listed restrictions of managed user accounts under Enterprise Managed Users.

choicesExplained.She can, once her IdP approves it: The docs state the restriction without an approval route.
choicesExplained.She can, but only with 2FA on: 2FA has nothing to do with this restriction.
choicesExplained.She can create public content but not co: Both public content and outside collaboration are ruled out.

notes.evidence: Managed user accounts cannot create public content or collaborate outside your enterprise.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”

notes.front: For Enterprise Managed Users, what do the docs advise about partner IdPs?
notes.back: Use a single partner IdP for both authentication and provisioning.
notes.explanation: The docs say this simplifies configuration and ensures full support.
notes.evidence: To simplify your configuration and ensure full support, use a single partner IdP for both authentication and provisioning.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “How does EMUs integrate with identity management systems?”

notes.front: An enterprise owner has disabled a Copilot feature everywhere. An organization owner in that enterprise wants to turn it on for her organization. What happens?
choices: She cannot override the enterprise setting at organization level
Both settings apply and users choose
She can turn it on for selected repositories only
notes.back: She cannot override the enterprise setting at organization level.
notes.explanation: Copilot policies are also managed at enterprise level, and a specific enterprise policy cannot be overridden by an organization.

choicesExplained.Her organization setting takes precedenc: The enterprise owner's specific policy wins over the organization.
choicesExplained.Both settings apply and users choose: The docs describe no such user choice.
choicesExplained.She can turn it on for selected reposito: The enterprise has disabled the feature everywhere, which the organization cannot override.

notes.evidence: If your enterprise owner has selected a specific policy, such as enabling a feature everywhere, disabling it everywhere, or enabling it for selected organizations only, you cannot override that setting at the organization level.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization”

notes.front: In an organization's Copilot settings, what does the Models page control?
notes.back: Availability of models beyond the basic models provided with Copilot, which may incur additional costs.
notes.explanation: The Policies page, by contrast, controls privacy and the availability of features.
notes.evidence: Click Policies to edit the policies that control privacy and availability of features. * Click Models to edit the policies that control availability of models beyond the basic models provided with Copilot, which may incur additional costs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization”, “Enabling Copilot features and models in your organization”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: Who can access a public repository, and who can access a private one?
notes.back: Public: everyone on the internet. Private: you, people you explicitly share with and, for organization repositories, certain members.
notes.explanation: For organization repositories, certain organization members can also reach private ones.
notes.evidence: Public repositories are accessible to everyone on the internet. * Private repositories are only accessible to you, people you explicitly share access with, and, for organization repositories, certain organization members.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About repositories”, “About repository visibility”

notes.front: A developer on GitHub Free wants to create an internal repository on her personal account. Can she?
choices: No: internal visibility is for repositories in organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud owned by an enterprise account
Yes: any repository can be internal
Only if the repository is a template repository
notes.back: No: internal visibility is only for repositories in organizations that use GitHub Enterprise Cloud and are owned by an enterprise account.
notes.explanation: Otherwise, a repository is public or private when you create it.

choicesExplained.Yes: any repository can be internal: Only repositories in enterprise-owned organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud can be internal.
choicesExplained.Yes, if she turns on 2FA: 2FA does not change which visibilities are available.
choicesExplained.Only if the repository is a template rep: Being a template has nothing to do with internal visibility.

notes.evidence: When you create a repository, you can choose to make the repository public or private. Repositories in organizations that use GitHub Enterprise Cloud and are owned by an enterprise account can also be created with internal visibility.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About repositories”, “About repository visibility”

notes.front: What file do the docs say you should add to a public repository to explain how to report vulnerabilities?
notes.back: A security policy: a SECURITY.md file.
notes.explanation: The docs pair this with turning on security features such as Dependabot, secret scanning, push protection and code scanning.
notes.evidence: You can mitigate these risks by enabling GitHub security features such as Dependabot, secret scanning, push protection, and code scanning for the repository. Additionally, you should add a security policy (a SECURITY.md file) to your repository, that outlines how vulnerabilities should be reported
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About repositories”, “Security considerations for repository visibility”

notes.front: What happens to a repository's stars and watchers when you change it from public to private?
notes.back: They are erased, which affects repository rankings.
notes.explanation: The docs list this among the consequences to understand before changing visibility.
notes.evidence: Changing from public to private * Stars and watchers for this repository will be erased, which will affect repository rankings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting repository visibility”, “Changing from public to private”

notes.front: What are two consequences of changing a repository from private to public?
notes.back: Any two of: the code is visible to everyone; Actions history and logs become visible; all push rulesets are disabled; stars and watchers are erased.
notes.explanation: The docs list these, among others, under changing from private to public.
notes.evidence: Changing from private to public * The code will be visible to everyone who can visit GitHub.com. * Anyone can fork your repository. * All push rulesets will be disabled. * Your changes will be published as activity. * Actions history and logs will be visible to everyone. * Stars and watchers for this repository will be erased.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting repository visibility”, “Changing from private to public”

notes.front: When a repository changes from private to internal, who gets read access?
notes.back: All members of the enterprise.
notes.explanation: Its stars and watchers are also erased.
notes.evidence: Changing from private to internal * All members of the enterprise will be given read access. * Outside collaborators can no longer be added to forks unless they're added to the root. * Stars and watchers for this repository will be erased.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Setting repository visibility”, “Changing from private to internal”

notes.front: What two restrictions does every branch protection rule apply by default?
notes.back: It disables force pushes to the matching branches and prevents them from being deleted.
notes.explanation: You can optionally disable these restrictions and turn on further settings.
notes.evidence: By default, each branch protection rule disables force pushes to the matching branches and prevents the matching branches from being deleted. You can optionally disable these restrictions and enable additional branch protection settings.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “About branch protection rules”

notes.front: By default, do the restrictions of a branch protection rule apply to people with admin permissions to the repository?
notes.back: No, but you can optionally apply them to administrators too.
notes.explanation: The same default exemption covers custom roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission.
notes.evidence: By default, the restrictions of a branch protection rule don't apply to people with admin permissions to the repository or custom roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission. You can optionally apply the restrictions to administrators and roles with the "bypass branch protections" permission, too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “About branch protection rules”

notes.front: A team wants one branch protection rule to cover every branch whose name contains "hotfix". What can it do?
choices: Create a rule with an fnmatch name pattern such as *hotfix*
Create one rule per branch by hand
Protect all branches instead; patterns are not allowed
notes.back: Create a rule with an fnmatch name pattern such as *hotfix*.
notes.explanation: A rule can target a specific branch, all branches, or any branch matching an fnmatch name pattern.

choicesExplained.Create one rule per branch by hand: A single rule with a name pattern covers all matching branches.
choicesExplained.Protect all branches instead; patterns a: Name patterns in fnmatch syntax are allowed.
choicesExplained.Use a label called hotfix: Labels categorise issues, pull requests and discussions; they do not protect branches.

notes.evidence: You can create a branch protection rule in a repository for a specific branch, all branches, or any branch that matches a name pattern you specify with fnmatch syntax.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “About branch protection rules”

notes.front: Only {{c1::a single}} branch protection rule can apply to a branch at a time.
notes.back: a single
notes.explanation: So it can be hard to know which rule applies when several target the same branch; the restriction does not apply to rulesets.
notes.evidence: Only a single branch protection rule can apply at a time, which means it can be difficult to know which rule will apply when multiple versions of a rule target the same branch. This restriction does not apply to rulesets
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “About branch protection rules”

notes.front: Which branch protection setting requires a set number of approving reviews before a pull request is merged into a protected branch?
notes.back: Require pull request reviews before merging.
notes.explanation: You can require the approving reviews from people with write permissions or from a designated code owner.
notes.evidence: Repository administrators or custom roles with the "edit repository rules" permission can require that all pull requests receive a specific number of approving reviews before someone merges the pull request into a protected branch. You can require approving reviews from people with write permissions in the repository or from a designated code owner.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require pull request reviews before merging”

notes.front: Which branch protection setting makes checks reach a successful, skipped or neutral status before collaborators can change a protected branch?
notes.back: Require status checks before merging.
notes.explanation: Required status checks can be checks or commit statuses.
notes.evidence: Required status checks must have a successful , skipped , or neutral status before collaborators can make changes to a protected branch. Required status checks can be checks or commit statuses.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require status checks before merging”

notes.front: Which branch protection setting lets contributors and bots push only signed and verified commits?
notes.back: Require signed commits.
notes.explanation: The rule covers bots as well as human contributors.
notes.evidence: When you enable required commit signing on a branch, contributors and bots can only push commits that have been signed and verified to the branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require signed commits”

notes.front: A team wants no merge commits on main, so that every pull request lands by squash or rebase. Which branch protection setting should it turn on?
notes.back: Require linear history.
notes.explanation: Enforcing a linear history stops merge commits being pushed, so pull requests into the branch must use a squash or rebase merge.

choicesExplained.Lock branch: Locking makes the branch read-only, so nothing could land at all.
choicesExplained.Require signed commits: This requires signed, verified commits; it does not ban merge commits.
choicesExplained.Require conversation resolution before m: This requires comments to be resolved; it does not ban merge commits.

notes.evidence: Enforcing a linear commit history prevents collaborators from pushing merge commits to the branch. This means that any pull requests merged into the protected branch must use a squash merge or a rebase merge.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Require linear history”

notes.front: Which branch protection setting makes a branch read-only, so no commits can be made to it?
notes.back: Lock branch.
notes.explanation: A locked branch also cannot be deleted.
notes.evidence: Locking a branch will make the branch read-only and ensures that no commits can be made to the branch. Locked branches can also not be deleted.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About protected branches”, “Lock branch”

notes.front: Who can give a team access to organization repositories, and at what levels?
notes.back: Organization owners and team maintainers can give teams admin, read or write access.
notes.explanation: Teams are used to manage access for people in an organization, and for notifications.
notes.evidence: You can use teams to manage access for people in an organization, and for sending notifications. Organization owners and team maintainers can give teams admin, read, or write access to organization repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “About teams”

notes.front: An organization member needs to alert everyone on the design team about a pull request, in one comment. What can she do?
choices: Add each person as an assignee
notes.back: Mention the team's name.
notes.explanation: Organization members can send a notification to a whole team by mentioning the team's name.

choicesExplained.Add each person as an assignee: Assignees show who is working on an item; they are not a way to alert a team.
choicesExplained.Apply a label named design: A label categorises the pull request; it does not notify a team.
choicesExplained.Create a saved reply: A saved reply is reusable text, not a team notification.

notes.evidence: Organization members can send a notification to an entire team by mentioning the team's name.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “About teams”

notes.front: Can an outside collaborator be on a team?
notes.back: No: teams can only be made up of members of your organization.
notes.explanation: Teams are groups of organization members, and the docs state that outside collaborators are unable to be on one.
notes.evidence: Teams can only be made up of members of your organization, outside collaborators are unable to be on a team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “About teams”

notes.front: What is the difference between a visible team and a secret team?
notes.back: Every organization member can view and @mention a visible team; a secret team is visible only to its members and organization owners.
notes.explanation: The docs suggest secret teams for hiding the members of teams that work with external partners or clients.
notes.evidence: Visible teams can be viewed and @mentioned by every organization member. * Secret teams are only visible to the people on the team and organization owners. They're great for hiding the members of teams that work with external partners or clients.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “Team visibility”

notes.front: An organization forms a team to work with a client and wants to hide who is on it from other members. It also plans to put the team under Engineering as a child team. Can it do both?
choices: No: a secret team hides members but cannot be nested
Yes: make it a secret child team
Yes: make it a visible child team
notes.back: No: a secret team hides its members, but secret teams cannot be nested under parent teams.
notes.explanation: Secret teams suit teams working with external partners or clients, and they cannot have parent or child teams.

choicesExplained.Yes: make it a secret child team: Secret teams cannot be nested under parent teams.
choicesExplained.Yes: make it a visible child team: A visible team can be viewed by every organization member, so its members are not hidden.
choicesExplained.No: teams cannot have parents: Visible teams can be nested under parent teams.

notes.evidence: They're great for hiding the members of teams that work with external partners or clients. However, if a team member or organization owner mentions a secret team, the team name is visible in the mention text. Secret teams cannot be nested under parent teams or have child teams.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “Team visibility”

notes.front: The Support team has two child teams, Billing Support and Tech Support. An owner grants Support write access to a repository. Which teams get write access?
choices: Support, Billing Support and Tech Support
None until each child team is granted access
notes.back: Support, Billing Support and Tech Support.
notes.explanation: Child teams inherit the parent team's access permissions.

choicesExplained.Only Support: Child teams inherit the parent's access permissions.
choicesExplained.Only the two child teams: The parent team itself was granted the access.
choicesExplained.None until each child team is granted ac: Inheritance means no separate grant is needed.

notes.evidence: Child teams inherit the parent's access permissions, simplifying permissions management for large groups.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “Nested teams”

notes.front: When a parent team is @mentioned, who is notified?
notes.back: Members of the parent team and of its child teams.
notes.explanation: The docs say this simplifies communication with multiple groups of people.
notes.evidence: Members of child teams also receive notifications when the parent team is @mentioned, simplifying communication with multiple groups of people.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About organization teams”, “Nested teams”
